title: Jeremiah 25:30–38
context: Jeremiah is told to prophesy that “The LORD will roar from on high,” shouting like those who tread grapes against all the inhabitants of the earth, for “the LORD has a controversy with the nations.” The LORD of Armies describes evil going out from nation to nation like a storm, the slain lying unburied, and the shepherds, the leaders of the flock, wailing because the LORD destroys their pasture and has left his covert like a lion. The roar recalls Amos 1:2, and both traditions share the ground that God’s judgment is just and universal, while the “evil” going out points to the existing box at Judges 9:23 rather than a new one.

verses.text: “Therefore prophesy against them all these words, and tell them, “ ‘The LORD will roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation. He will mightily roar against his fold. He will give a shout, as those who tread grapes, against all the inhabitants of the earth.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah is told to say, “The LORD will roar from on high, and utter his voice from his holy habitation.” Arminian readers note the image of a lion and the echo of Amos 1:2.

The shout “as those who tread grapes” pictures judgment as a harvest.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the majesty and terror of God’s judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the roar as poetic language for the LORD’s active judgment, which reaches “all the inhabitants of the earth.”

verses.text: A noise will come even to the end of the earth; for the LORD has a controversy with the nations. He will enter into judgment with all flesh. As for the wicked, he will give them to the sword,” ’ says the LORD.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The oracle continues, “for the LORD has a controversy with the nations. He will enter into judgment with all flesh.” Arminian readers note the courtroom language.

The judgment is a legal case, not arbitrary violence.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God as the righteous judge of all the earth.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God judges justly and that “the wicked” are named as those given to the sword.

verses.text: The LORD of Armies says, “Behold, evil will go out from nation to nation, and a great storm will be raised up from the uttermost parts of the earth.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD of Armies says, “Behold, evil will go out from nation to nation, and a great storm will be raised up.” Arminian readers take “evil” as calamity spreading through the nations.

The storm image conveys its force.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the calamity as under God’s governance.

Shared ground: both traditions keep the existing box at Judges 9:23 in view rather than restating it, and agree that God remains just in judging the nations.

verses.text: The slain of the LORD will be at that day from one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth. They won’t be lamented. They won’t be gathered or buried. They will be dung on the surface of the ground.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The slain of the LORD will be at that day from one end of the earth even to the other end of the earth.” Arminian readers note the breadth of the judgment.

The lack of mourning and burial marks utter disgrace.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise read the verse soberly as a picture of judgment’s reach.

Shared ground: both traditions handle the imagery without expansion, agreeing that it warns of the seriousness of sin before a holy God.

verses.text: Wail, you shepherds, and cry. Wallow in dust, you leader of the flock; for the days of your slaughter and of your dispersions have fully come, and you will fall like fine pottery.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Wail, you shepherds, and cry. Wallow in dust, you leader of the flock.” Arminian readers note that the shepherds are the rulers of the nations.

Those who led others are now humbled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see leaders held accountable for their charge (cf. 23:1–2).

Shared ground: both traditions agree that rulers answer to God, and that the image of fine pottery falling conveys how quickly their glory is broken.

verses.text: The shepherds will have no way to flee. The leader of the flock will have no escape.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The shepherds will have no way to flee. The leader of the flock will have no escape.” Arminian readers note the inescapable nature of the judgment.

Power offers no refuge.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s judgment reaching those who seemed secure.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a warning to all in authority that they cannot escape God’s reckoning.

verses.text: A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and the wailing of the leader of the flock, for the LORD destroys their pasture.
verses.arminianNotes:
“A voice of the cry of the shepherds, and the wailing of the leader of the flock, for the LORD destroys their pasture.” Arminian readers note the sound of lament.

The pasture is the land they ruled.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God as the one who brings down the rulers’ domains.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as poetry about real loss, and both note the contrast with the faithful shepherd God promises elsewhere (cf. 23:4).

verses.text: The peaceful folds are brought to silence because of the fierce anger of the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The peaceful folds are brought to silence because of the fierce anger of the LORD.” Arminian readers note the stillness after judgment.

Places once at peace are emptied.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the reality of God’s holy anger against sin.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s anger is not capricious but a just response to persistent evil, as the chapter has explained.

verses.text: He has left his covert, as the lion; for their land has become an astonishment because of the fierceness of the oppression, and because of his fierce anger.
verses.arminianNotes:
“He has left his covert, as the lion.” Arminian readers note that the chapter returns to the lion image of 25:30.

The land becomes “an astonishment because of the fierceness of the oppression.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the LORD as the one who acts in judgment.

Shared ground: both traditions read the closing image soberly and note that the oppression described is carried out through human armies under God’s rule.
